transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I’m here because at work I keep losing my train of thought, and it’s getting hard to manage. I’m a nurse, and on the floor there’s always something—an IV pump beeping, someone asking another nurse a question, a call light going off—and then suddenly I can’t remember what patient flow issue I was in the middle of handling. It’s happening a lot, and it’s really affecting me.
Did you have this same kind of trouble staying focused when you were a child?

Yes, I did. Even in elementary school, teachers would say I was bright, but careless. I was always losing worksheets or forgetting to turn in homework. My mom had to sit with me pretty much every night just to keep me on track.
Outside of work, do you also have the same kind of trouble staying focused in your day-to-day life?

Yes, I do, but the biggest place I notice it is at work. On the floor I lose my train of thought constantly. Like, an IV pump beeps, someone asks another nurse something, or a call light goes off, and suddenly I’ve forgotten what patient flow issue I was handling. It’s like my focus just gets pulled away and I can’t get back to where I was.
When did these concentration problems first start?
It really became a major problem when I took on the expanded charge-nurse responsibilities, almost two years ago. I’d had trouble before, but that’s when it started seriously affecting me day to day.
Have you been feeling depressed معظم اليوم nearly every day?
I don’t think so. I mean, I get frustrated and overwhelmed, but I wouldn’t say I’ve been depressed most of the day nearly every day.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot, even when there isn’t an immediate problem to handle?
I’m not sure I’d call it worrying a lot. I do think about things I need to handle, but it’s not like I’m sitting there anxious when nothing is going on.
Do you often act or speak before thinking?
I don’t think that’s a big issue for me. I’m usually not blurting things out or acting impulsively, at least not that I’ve noticed.
Do you often feel restless, like it’s hard to sit still?
Not really. I mean, I can sit still when I need to. I might shift around a little, but I don’t feel like I’m driven to move or anything like that.
Have you had any head injury, seizure, or other neurologic illness?
Not that I know of. I haven’t had any seizures or neurologic illness, and I don’t remember any significant head injury.
Did these concentration problems begin after a particularly stressful event or major life change?
It wasn’t really after one single stressful event. It became a major problem when I took on expanded charge-nurse responsibilities, almost two years ago. Since then it’s been pretty significant.
Do these focus problems cause significant problems for you in settings other than work, such as at home or in daily responsibilities?

Yes. It definitely shows up at home and with regular responsibilities too. I forget things that should be routine, like calling a family member back or paying a bill, and I’ve missed appointments even when I meant to go. Sometimes I’ll even set a reminder and still somehow not follow through. It’s frustrating because these aren’t things I don’t care about—I just lose track of them.
Do you find yourself unable to control or stop worrying?
I don’t think so, not in a constant way. I worry about things, especially if I’ve forgotten something, but I wouldn’t say it feels uncontrollable most of the time.
Before age 12, did these attention problems ever cause problems for you at school?

Yes, it did. Even back in elementary school, teachers would say I was bright but careless. I was always losing worksheets or forgetting to turn in homework. My mom had to sit with me most nights just to keep me on track.
Do you often have trouble staying focused when reading or doing paperwork?

Yes, definitely. If I know something is going to take a lot of focused reading or paperwork, I tend to put it off. Like with chart reviews or auditing documentation across shifts, I’ll keep finding bedside tasks to do instead, because sitting down and staying with it feels almost impossible—like trying to climb a wall.
Do you often find your mind drifting when someone is speaking directly to you?
I’m not totally sure. I mean, sometimes I lose the thread of what someone’s saying, but I haven’t really paid attention to whether it happens when they’re speaking directly to me.
When someone is speaking directly to you, do you often find that your mind wanders and you miss part of what they said?
I’m honestly not sure. I notice sometimes I miss pieces of what people say, but I don’t know if it’s specifically when they’re talking directly to me or if it’s more just in general.
Do you often avoid tasks that require a lot of sustained mental effort?

Yes. If I know something is going to take a lot of focused effort, especially chart review or auditing documentation across shifts, I keep putting it off. I’ll find bedside tasks to do instead, because sitting down and staying with it feels really hard—like trying to climb a wall.
Do you often have trouble organizing tasks or keeping your work and responsibilities in order?

Yes, definitely. When I’m charge nurse, I’ll have scraps of paper, sticky notes, half-started lists everywhere, and I still can’t get it organized in my head. I have a hard time deciding what needs to happen first, so I end up just reacting to whatever problem is loudest, and then I’m rushing at the end of the shift to catch up.
Do you often start tasks but then fail to finish them, even when you intend to complete them?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I do start things and sometimes they don’t get done right away, but I haven’t noticed a clear pattern of starting tasks and not finishing them. I’d have to think about that more.
Do you often have trouble following through on tasks, so that things get started but don’t get finished?

I’m still not sure I’d say that exactly. I do sometimes delay things or have trouble keeping track of them, but I haven’t really noticed a consistent pattern where I start tasks and then just don’t finish them. I’d need to think about specific examples.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a longstanding pattern of inattentive symptoms beginning in childhood, present across multiple settings (work and home), and causing functional impairment. Confirmed features include distractibility, forgetfulness, disorganization, and avoidance of tasks requiring sustained mental effort. Hyperactive/impulsive symptoms are not prominent, supporting predominantly inattentive ADHD rather than anxiety- or stress-related conditions. Generalized anxiety was not supported by uncontrollable excessive worry, and no discrete traumatic or major stress-related precipitant was identified.
